questions.question: What is React, and what problem does it solve?
questions.title: React and its component model
questions.direct_answer: React is a JavaScript library for rendering user interfaces from reusable components. A component describes what the UI should look like for its current props and state; when that data changes, React renders again and commits the required DOM updates. It is especially useful for interactive interfaces with shared, changing data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands React as a declarative component model rather than a collection of DOM shortcuts.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling React a complete framework or claiming that every render rebuilds the whole browser DOM.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate rendering from committing and explain when a plain server-rendered page may not need much React.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: React is a library for rendering user interfaces.
A React UI is composed from reusable, nestable components.
Components describe output from props, state, and context.
A state update triggers rendering; React then commits required DOM changes.
React does not provide every application feature by itself.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. A component is a JavaScript function that receives inputs such as props and returns a description of the UI, usually written with JSX. Components can be nested, so a page becomes a tree of smaller pieces such as Header, ProductList, and ProductCard.

The main idea is declarative rendering. Instead of manually finding a DOM node and issuing commands whenever data changes, the component describes the desired screen for the current props and state. When state changes, React calls the relevant component functions again, works out the next element tree, and commits the DOM changes needed to make the browser match it.

For example, a cart button can render `Cart (2)` from a `count` state value. Calling its setter requests another render with `count` equal to three. The component describes `Cart (3)`, and React updates the text in the committed DOM; the application code does not need to locate that text node itself.

React also gives a predictable direction for data. Parents pass values down as props, and children report user actions through callback props. Local state records information that must survive between renders. Keeping render logic pure makes the same inputs produce the same JSX and lets React safely repeat or interrupt rendering work.

React is not a complete application framework by itself. Routing, data loading, deployment, and server rendering usually come from other libraries or a React framework. A mostly static document may be simpler as semantic HTML with a small script rather than a full React application. So I choose React when the interface has reusable views and coordinated state, and I describe its value as a component and rendering model—not as magic that replaces HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or the DOM.

sections.title: Describe the screen, not the DOM commands
sections.content: React turns current application data into a tree of elements. The browser still displays ordinary DOM nodes, but application code normally describes the desired result through components instead of keeping many manual DOM operations in sync.

sections.title: The two phases behind an update
sections.content:
During **rendering**, React calls components to calculate the next UI description. Render code should only calculate: it must not send requests, change existing objects, or depend on which component renders first.

During **commit**, React applies the necessary changes to the host environment, such as the browser DOM. A component can render again without its DOM changing when the returned output is equivalent. Effects that synchronize external systems run after a commit, not during the pure render calculation.

sections.title: A state-driven UI update
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[User event] --> B[Queue state update]
  B --> C[Render component tree]
  C --> D[Compare with previous output]
  D --> E[Commit needed DOM changes]
  E --> F[Browser shows updated UI]
```

sections.title: Describe one button from state
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Do not describe React as replacing the DOM or updating only one node in every possible case. React calculates UI descriptions and decides how to commit them. The size and cost of an update depend on component structure, state placement, keys, and the renderer.

questions.question: What is JSX, and how is it different from HTML?
questions.title: JSX syntax and HTML differences
questions.direct_answer: JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension for writing HTML-like element descriptions inside JavaScript. A build tool transforms it into JavaScript calls that create React elements. It resembles HTML, but expressions use braces, many DOM properties use JavaScript names such as `className`, tags must close, and a component must return one root value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can explain JSX as compiled JavaScript and apply its essential syntax rules.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling JSX HTML or assuming the browser parses it directly.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the compiled shape and explain why custom component names begin with a capital letter.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: JSX is syntax for element descriptions; it is not an HTML string.
A compiler transforms JSX into JavaScript before it runs.
Use `{expression}` to insert a JavaScript expression.
Use JavaScript-style property names such as `className` and `onClick`.
Close every tag and wrap sibling roots in an element or Fragment.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
JSX is a syntax extension used to describe React elements with HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. The browser does not normally execute JSX directly. A compiler such as Babel, SWC, or the framework's build tool transforms it into JavaScript calls for the JSX runtime, producing plain element objects that React can render. JSX looks familiar, but it follows JavaScript and DOM conventions in several places. JavaScript expressions go inside curly braces, event properties use camelCase such as `onClick`, and the CSS class property is `className`. Every element must close, including tags such as ``, because JSX must form an unambiguous expression. A component returns one JavaScript value, so adjacent top-level elements need a common element or a Fragment. A Fragment groups siblings without adding another DOM node. Lowercase tag names represent host elements such as `button`; capitalized names such as `ProductCard` refer to JavaScript component variables. For example, `

{product.name}: {product.price}

` combines static markup with values from a JavaScript object. The braces can contain expressions such as property access, function calls, or a conditional expression, but not statements such as `if` or `for` directly inside the markup. JSX is optional—React elements can be created without it—but JSX usually keeps rendering structure near the logic that supplies its values. It also does not remove the need for valid semantics: a JSX `div` is still a neutral DOM `div`, while a JSX `button` still carries native button behaviour. The useful mental model is that JSX is readable source syntax that becomes JavaScript data. React consumes that data; the browser ultimately receives normal DOM nodes, attributes, text, and event behaviour.

sections.title: Markup-shaped JavaScript
sections.content: JSX lets a component place the structure and the values that produce it close together. It is parsed as part of JavaScript source, transformed during the build, and represented as element objects at runtime rather than injected as an unchecked HTML string.

sections.title: Why the syntax rules differ
sections.content:
An opening JSX tag begins a nested JavaScript expression. The parser therefore needs explicit closing tags and a single enclosing value. Braces temporarily return from markup-like syntax to JavaScript expression syntax.

Property names follow the React DOM API, which is why `className`, `htmlFor`, and camel-cased event names appear. Most ordinary `data-*` and `aria-*` attributes keep their lowercase dashed spelling. A capitalized tag must resolve to a variable in scope; a lowercase tag is treated as a platform element name.

sections.title: HTML source and JSX source
sections.content: | Concern | HTML source | JSX source | |---|---|---| | CSS class | `class="card"` | `className="card"` | | Dynamic value | Template/server syntax | `{product.name}` | | Click handler | Usually added with JavaScript | `onClick={handleClick}` | | Empty element | `` is allowed | `` must close | | Sibling roots | Document can have many | Return one wrapper or Fragment |

sections.title: From JSX to an element description
Boundary to remember
sections.content: JSX escapes ordinary string values before inserting them, but it cannot make every operation safe. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` deliberately bypasses that protection and requires trusted or correctly sanitized HTML. JSX syntax also does not guarantee accessible markup; element choice still matters.

questions.question: Which JavaScript values can React render inside JSX?
questions.title: JavaScript expressions and values in JSX
questions.direct_answer: Inside JSX braces, React can render strings and numbers as text, React elements as UI, and arrays of renderable values as siblings. `null`, `undefined`, and booleans render nothing. Plain objects are not valid children. Braces accept expressions, so statements such as `if` and `for` must run before the returned JSX.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands JSX expression boundaries and React child values.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Rendering an object directly or using `count && <Badge />` when zero must remain visible.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain boolean rendering and the zero-value conditional trap with a concrete trace.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Strings and numbers become text nodes.
Elements and arrays of renderable values produce UI.
`null`, `undefined`, `true`, and `false` render nothing.
A plain object cannot be rendered directly as a child.
Braces contain expressions, not `if`, `for`, or variable declarations.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Curly braces in JSX open a JavaScript expression. The expression is evaluated first, and React then interprets its result as a child or property value. Strings and numbers render as text. A React element renders its described subtree, and an array of renderable entries can become several siblings when their identity is handled correctly.

`null`, `undefined`, `true`, and `false` do not create visible children. That makes expressions such as `isAdmin && <AdminTools />` convenient. However, the left side of `&&` is returned when it is falsy, so `count && <Badge />` renders the number zero when `count` is `0`. A boolean comparison such as `count > 0 && <Badge />` avoids that surprise.

A plain JavaScript object is not a valid React child because React does not know how the object should be presented. I render one property, map the object to elements, or serialize it intentionally for debugging. Objects are valid as prop values and as style objects; the restriction is about placing the object itself where a child should be.

For example, a message panel can display `{user.name}`, conditionally show an unread badge, and map `messages` into keyed `Message` components. The expression can call `filter`, `map`, or a helper function, but complex transformations are usually clearer when calculated in a named variable above the return.

Braces accept expressions that produce a value. Statements such as `if`, `switch`, `for`, and `const` declarations do not produce a value in that position, so they belong before the JSX or inside a helper. Ternaries are useful for two visible alternatives; `&&` works best for show-or-show-nothing conditions. The boundary is readability and value shape: compute complex decisions outside the markup, deliberately handle empty and zero values, and turn application objects into meaningful elements instead of asking React to guess their presentation.

sections.title: Evaluate first, then render the result
sections.content: JSX does not display the source text between braces. JavaScript evaluates the expression, and React receives the returned value. Understanding that returned value explains why strings appear, booleans disappear, arrays expand, and plain objects fail.

sections.title: Conditional expressions preserve their real values
sections.content:
JavaScript's `&&` operator does not return a special boolean. It returns the first falsy operand or the last operand. Therefore `0 && <Badge />` evaluates to `0`, and React faithfully renders that number. `false && <Badge />` evaluates to `false`, which React omits.

Arrays are flattened into sibling children. When those children can be inserted, removed, or reordered, stable keys let React match each new child to its earlier identity. The array is renderable, but its items still need sensible element structure and identity.

sections.title: What a JSX child becomes
sections.content:
| Expression result | Visible result |
|---|---|
| `'Ready'` | Text `Ready` |
| `0` | Text `0` |
| `false`, `null`, `undefined` | Nothing |
| `<Badge />` | Badge subtree |
| `[<A />, <B />]` | Sibling subtrees |
| `{ status: 'ok' }` | Error: object is not a valid child |

sections.title: Handle empty and zero values deliberately
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Do not hide meaningful zero values by converting every condition to a boolean. A shopping cart may need to display `0 items`. Choose a ternary, an explicit comparison, or direct number rendering according to the intended UI.

questions.question: What happens during React's render and commit phases?
questions.title: React render and commit phases
questions.direct_answer: A React update has a render phase, where React calls components and calculates the next UI tree, and a commit phase, where it applies the required changes to the DOM. Rendering must stay pure because React may repeat or abandon it. DOM work and Effect setup happen only after React commits the chosen result.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner distinguishes component calculation from browser mutation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying that every component call immediately writes to the DOM or running side effects during render.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that a render can produce no DOM change and that type and key help React match identities.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A trigger schedules work: initial mount, state update, or parent render.
Render calls components to calculate the next element tree.
Reconciliation matches the next tree with the previous tree.
Commit applies required DOM changes.
Effects run after a commit; render code must remain pure.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
React separates an update into rendering and committing. An initial root render, a component state update, or a parent update can schedule rendering. In the render phase, React calls component functions and uses their returned elements to calculate what the UI should be for the latest inputs.

Rendering is a calculation, not a DOM operation. React compares the new element structure with the previous one, matching children primarily by their element type and position, with keys providing identity inside collections. This reconciliation tells React which host nodes can be reused, which properties changed, and which subtrees must be added or removed.

In the commit phase, React applies the chosen changes to the DOM. If a component renders the same effective output, the component function may have run while the corresponding DOM remains unchanged. This is why ‘render’ and ‘DOM update’ are not synonyms.

For example, changing a counter from two to three makes React render the component with a new state snapshot. Its next tree contains the same button element with different text. During commit React can keep the button node and update its text instead of replacing the whole page.

Render logic must stay pure because React may call it more than once, pause it, or discard work before commit. Changing external variables, starting network requests, or mutating props during render would make those repeated calculations observable and unpredictable. User-caused work belongs in event handlers, while synchronization caused by rendering belongs in an Effect. After commit, the browser can paint the updated interface and React can run appropriate Effects. The practical model is: trigger, calculate a pure next tree, reconcile identity, commit host changes, then synchronize external systems.

sections.title: Calculation and mutation are separate
sections.content: A component call answers a question: given these inputs, what element tree is desired? React can calculate that answer without touching the browser. Only a committed result is allowed to change host nodes or start the Effect lifecycle.

sections.title: Identity guides reconciliation
sections.content:
When the element type stays the same in the same position, React can usually update that existing subtree. A different type normally replaces the old subtree. Within lists, a key extends identity beyond a raw position so an item can move without being mistaken for a different item.

This model also explains state preservation. React associates state with a component's position and identity in the render tree. Keeping the same identity preserves its state; changing its type or key can intentionally reset it.

sections.title: One counter update
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant E as Event handler
  participant R as React render
  participant C as Commit
  participant D as Browser DOM
  E->>R: queue count = 3
  R->>R: calculate next element tree
  R->>C: changed text in same button
  C->>D: update text node
```

sections.title: A render can leave most DOM untouched
Boundary to remember
sections.content: Reconciliation is an implementation strategy, not permission to ignore render cost. Expensive calculations still run when a component renders unless the structure or an appropriate optimization avoids them. Measure a real problem before adding memoization everywhere.
